title: Democrats target Trump’s tariffs. Can they agree on what’s next?
text:
Democrats target Trump’s tariffs. Can they agree on what’s next?
Democrats have won a mandate to tackle affordability, but efforts to reverse President Trump’s tariffs could expose divisions within their party.
When Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed was asked this week about what Democrats in Congress should do about affordability, he had a pithy answer. “End the war. Stop the tariffs,” he told NPR.
Both the war with Iran and gyrating U.S. tariffs are signature policies of President Donald Trump that proved to be broadly unpopular with voters. Now the incoming Democratic majority is weighing what measures Congress can pass to foist change on his administration, starting with lifting punitive tariffs on Canada, which even Republicans running in border states such as Michigan and Maine repudiated during the campaign.
By targeting Mr. Trump’s tariffs, which two-thirds of midterm voters in an exit poll said had hurt the economy, Democrats see an opening to shape an affordability agenda. Voters who may have once associated tariffs with support for American jobs now blame those duties for higher prices.
But how exactly Democrats constrain a president who has creatively used decades-old trade laws to impose levies on imports is unclear. After the Supreme Court ruled in February that the application of one emergency statute to enact the fees was unlawful, the administration pivoted to others, including a rarely used provision of the 1930 Tariff Act used to impose 50% tariffs on Canadian goods. Mr. Trump is likely to veto any legislation that restricts his authority to impose tariffs. (On Thursday, he threatened to double tariffs on Mexico amid reports of migrant caravans at the border.)
Congress is taking on President Donald Trump’s unpopular tariffs. But balancing trade policy, job protection, and business interests can be tricky, especially when some voters don’t believe free trade is always fair.
Mr. Trump isn’t the only protectionist in Washington. Some Democrats have long supported tariffs and argued that trade agreements should include safeguards for environmental and labor standards. When Mr. Trump first ran for president in 2016, his views on trade were closer to those of Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont, than his Republican primary opponents. Mr. Sanders remains a skeptic of free trade, as do many Democrats who represent industrial states where union support still matters. Democrats elected in farming states such as Iowa and Kansas, though, ran hard against Mr. Trump’s tariffs that have disrupted crop exports to China, costing farmers sales and leaving American farms at a disadvantage.
Swapping positions
“The economics point towards trying to reverse at least some of the tariffs,” says Michael Klein, a former economist in the U.S. Treasury who teaches at Tufts University. “There is a group within Congress from the industrial heartland that might favor tariffs, but given that [the tariffs] didn’t deliver, it’s easier for them to disavow them at this point.”
In some ways, the two parties have swapped positions on trade and tariffs. Under Mr. Trump, Republicans who once extolled the economic benefits of free trade supported U.S. tariffs that the administration said would revive industries, create jobs, and close the trade deficit. But their chaotic rollout in Mr. Trump’s second term, coupled with high inflation, proved a political loser and pushed Democrats to defend free trade, even as it remains a bugbear on the left as part of a broader critique of free-market economics.
In a postelection memo, the Congressional Progressive Caucus led by Rep. Greg Casar of Texas said its priorities included opposing Mr. Trump’s “blanket tariffs” but didn’t set out a position on trade policy. Mr. Sanders, who campaigned with Mr. El-Sayed in Michigan and with Maine Senator-elect Troy Jackson, hasn’t commented publicly on what Democrats in the Senate should do. Last year, he criticized Mr. Trump’s across-the-board levies but also said he supported targeted tariffs “that can help level the playing field” for U.S. workers by stopping corporations from outsourcing jobs.
“A complicated business”
Support on the left for some forms of trade protection remains strong, says Gary Gerstle, a historian and professor emeritus at the University of Cambridge who studies American political economy. Attempting to end all of Mr. Trump’s tariffs could splinter Democratic ranks. “The diverging interests between the industrial and the agricultural states to get this through Congress is a complicated business. They can’t make it their first piece of business,” says Professor Gerstle.
Democrats recognize that steelmakers and other unionized industries support tariffs as part of a broader trade strategy. “They’ll have to walk a tightrope in terms of how they frame their views and positions on tariffs,” says Chris Borick, a political scientist at Lehigh University in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania. Focusing on Canada as a first step toward placing broader restrictions on presidential tariff powers would be an easier political lift and allow Democrats to reassert the authority of Congress. “That’s low-hanging fruit in terms of public opinion in lots of key swing states that are right on the border,” he says.
After Mr. Trump’s first term, President Joe Biden chose to keep tariffs on China in place while working with Congress to fund expansive programs to support U.S. industries, including semiconductor manufacturing and clean-energy producers. Mr. Biden also imposed tariffs on Chinese electric cars, seeking to shield domestic automakers. Should Democrats legislate to curb Mr. Trump’s authority to impose tariffs except during strict emergencies, they would strip that same power from future Democratic presidents.
For now, Democrats face a president who has made tariffs central to his economic agenda. Mr. Trump has used tariffs both to gain leverage for trade negotiations and to pursue political goals, such as supporting the Bolsonaro family in Brazil. On Tuesday, CNBC reported that an administration official told a business conference in Washington that there would be no change in tariff policy, at least for the next two years. “Our ambition is to continue this pace for the remainder of the president’s term in office,” said Jim Goyer, who directs the White House Office of Public Liaison.
Trade policy matters
While Republicans in Congress who support free trade could side with Democrats trying to reverse specific tariffs, mustering enough votes to overturn a presidential veto would be a tall order. (Most legislation in the Senate still needs 60 votes to overcome a filibuster. If Mr. Trump vetoes a bill, overriding him requires a two-thirds vote in both chambers.)
Administration officials also cite higher customs revenue as a reason to maintain tariffs, though economists say the ultimate cost is borne by consumers who pay higher prices for goods.
Professor Klein says the Trump administration’s tariffs have soured voters on the idea of trade protection as an economic panacea.
Still, the political debate over trade policy is far from settled. “We’re certainly not in an era where people believe what they were told about the magic of tariffs in raising revenues and saving jobs and not affecting U.S. prices,’’ he says. “But my sense is there’s still a skepticism about complete global integration.”
